facts.quote: type_species: Asiatosuchus grangeri

facts.statement: Asiatosuchus species had a generalized crocodilian morphology characterized by flat, triangular skulls.
facts.quote: These species have a generalized crocodilian morphology typified by flat, triangular skulls.

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest that only the species A. grangeri belongs in the genus Asiatosuchus.
facts.quote: Recent studies of the evolutionary relationships of early crocodilians along with closer examinations of the morphology of fossil specimens suggest that only the first named species of Asiatosuchus, A. grangeri from the Eocene of Mongolia, belongs in the genus.

facts.statement: Most species previously assigned to Asiatosuchus are now regarded as nomina dubia because their type specimens lack unique anatomical features.
facts.quote: Most species are now regarded as nomina dubia or "dubious names", meaning that their type specimens lack the unique anatomical features necessary to justify their classification as distinct species.

facts.statement: Asiatosuchus had a generalized crocodilian skull that was triangular in shape when viewed from above.
facts.quote: Like most other Paleogene crocodyloids, Asiatosuchus has a generalized crocodilian skull that is triangular in shape when viewed from above.

facts.statement: Asiatosuchus species had teeth in the upper jaw that completely overlapped the teeth in the lower jaw, creating an overbite.
facts.quote: Asiatosuchus species have teeth in the upper jaw that completely overlap the teeth in the lower jaw, giving them overbites.

facts.statement: In Asiatosuchus, the mandibular symphysis is formed only by dentary bones, whereas in many other crocodyloids it involves dentary and splenial bones.
facts.quote: In many crocodyloids this joint is formed from two pairs of bones, the dentary bones and the splenial bones, but in Asiatosuchus it is only formed by the dentary bones.

facts.statement: Based on largely complete skeletons, Asiatosuchus may have grown up to 4 meters long.
facts.quote: Based on largely complete skeletons of "A." germanicus and "A." depressifrons, Asiatosuchus may have grown up to 4 m long.

facts.statement: The type species A. grangeri was named by paleontologist Charles Mook in 1940.
facts.quote: A. grangeri, the type species of Asiatosuchus, was named by paleontologist Charles Mook in 1940.

facts.statement: A. grangeri was named based on a lower jaw and skull fragments from the Middle Eocene Irdin Manha Formation in Inner Mongolia, China.
facts.quote: It was named on the basis of a lower jaw and pieces of a skull from the Irdin Manha Formation of Inner Mongolia, China, which dates back to the Middle Eocene.

facts.statement: The fossils of A. grangeri were discovered by the American Museum of Natural History's Central Asiatic Expedition of 1930 near Erenhot.
facts.quote: These fossils were discovered by the American Museum of Natural History's Central Asiatic Expedition of 1930 near Erenhot.

facts.statement: Mook named A. grangeri after Walter W. Granger, a vertebrate paleontologist and member of the expedition.
facts.quote: Mook named Asiatosuchus grangeri after Walter W. Granger, a vertebrate paleontologist with the American Museum of Natural History and a member of the expedition.

facts.statement: Well-preserved remains from Germany and France were described in 1966 and assigned to the new species A. germanicus.
facts.quote: Well-preserved remains of a crocodyloid were first described from Germany and France in 1966 and placed in a new species of Asiatosuchus, A. germanicus.

facts.statement: The German remains of A. germanicus came from the Messel Pit quarry, a site preserving life from Eocene anoxic lakes and subtropical forests.
facts.quote: The German remains came from the Messel Pit quarry, a fossil site that has preserved many forms of life that inhabited a series of anoxic lakes and surrounding subtropical forests during the Eocene.

facts.statement: A. germanicus is estimated to have reached a length of 6.5 meters (21.5 feet).
facts.quote: A.germanicus is estimated at 6.5 meters (21.5 ft) in length.

facts.statement: A. depressifrons was first named in 1855 as Crocodilus depressifrons.
facts.quote: "Asiatosuchus" depressifrons was first named in 1855 as Crocodilus depressifrons.

facts.statement: A. depressifrons was named based on a skull found in the Early Eocene Sables du Castrais Formation in France.
facts.quote: The naming of this new species was based on a skull found in the Sables du Castrais Formation, France that dates back to the Early Eocene.

facts.statement: In 1964, Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian named A. nanlingensis based on fragmentary material from the Shanghu Formation in Guangdong, China.
facts.quote: In 1964 Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian named a new species of Asiatosuchus, "A." nanlingensis, based on fragmentary material from the Shanghu Formation in Nanxiong, Guangdong Province, China.

facts.statement: It is debated whether A. nanlingensis and Eoalligator chunyii are synonymous, though some researchers agree they are the same species.
facts.quote: A. nanlingensis was discovered concurrently with the similar Eoalligator chunyii, and a 2016 study proposed that they are synonymous. A subsequent paper argued otherwise, but other researchers agree with the initial assessment synonymizing "A." nanlingensis and "E." chunyii.

facts.statement: Two species of Asiatosuchus were named from Russia: A. zajsanicus in 1982 and A. volgensis in 1993.
facts.quote: Two species of Asiatosuchus were named from Russia, A. zajsanicus in 1982 and A. volgensis in 1993.

facts.statement: A. volgensis and A. zajsanicus were regarded as nomina dubia because they are based on specimens with very little preserved anatomical detail.
facts.quote: A. volgensis and A. zajsanicus were regarded as nomina dubia by Angielczyk and Gingerich (1998) because they are based on fossil specimens that preserve very little anatomical detail.

facts.statement: A. zajsanicus was reassigned to Dollosuchus, though the validity of Dollosuchus itself is considered dubious by some.
facts.quote: A. zajsanicus was later reassigned to Dollosuchus, a genus of tomistomine crocodilians, by Efimov (1988), but Brochu (2007) treated Dollosuchus as dubious.

facts.statement: Several North American Paleogene crocodilian fossils have been proposed to belong to Asiatosuchus.
facts.quote: Several crocodilian fossils from the Paleogene of North America have also been proposed to belong to Asiatosuchus.

facts.statement: The classification of "C." affinis within Asiatosuchus is debated due to the fragmentary nature of A. grangeri's skull material.
facts.quote: Although "C." affinis is known from a complete skull, the skull material of A. grangeri is too fragmentary to support "C." affinis being classified within Asiatosuchus.

facts.statement: "C." monsvialensis was reassigned to Asiatosuchus in 1993, though subsequent authors questioned this and considered it synonymous with Diplocynodon ratelii.
facts.quote: "Crocodylus" monsvialensis was named from Early Oligocene deposits in Monteviale, Italy in 1914 and reassigned to Asiatosuchus in 1993, although subsequent authors questioned this referral and considered it synonymous with Diplocynodon ratelii.

facts.statement: "C." vicetinus was assigned to Asiatosuchus sp. in 2004, pending revision of the Monte Bolca material.
facts.quote: "Crocodylus" vicetinus from the Middle Eocene locality of Monte Bolca, was assigned to Asiatosuchus sp. by Kotsakis et al. (2004) pending revision of the Mount Bolca crocodilian material.

facts.statement: A partial crocodyloid skeleton from the Sulaiman Mountains of Pakistan was tentatively attributed to Asiatosuchus.
facts.quote: A partial skeleton of a crocodyloid from the Sulaiman Mountains of Pakistan was tentatively attributed to Asiatosuchus.

facts.statement: The Pakistani fossil was found in the Middle Eocene Drazinda Formation, a marine deposit that also preserved archaeocete whale remains.
facts.quote: The fossil was found in the Middle Eocene Drazinda Formation, a marine deposit which has also preserved the remains of archaeocete whales.

facts.statement: The presence of a possible Asiatosuchus specimen in marine deposits suggests these crocodilians could tolerate prolonged time in the ocean, aiding their dispersal across Europe and Asia.
facts.quote: The presence of a possible specimen of Asiatosuchus in marine deposits suggests that these crocodilians could have tolerated prolonged periods of time in the ocean, an ability that would have aided in the dispersal of early crocodyloids across Europe and Asia.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses classify Asiatosuchus as a member of the evolutionary group Crocodyloidea.
facts.quote: Phylogenetic analyses of the evolutionary relationships of crocodilians place Asiatosuchus as a member of a clade or evolutionary grouping called Crocodyloidea

facts.statement: Recent analyses place Asiatosuchus as a basal member of Crocodyloidea, near the evolutionary split from Alligatoroidea.
facts.quote: Recent phylogenetic analyses place Asiatosuchus as a basal ("primitive") member of this clade, close to the split between Crocodyloidea and Alligatoroidea

facts.statement: Most phylogenetic analyses suggest Asiatosuchus species form a paraphyletic grouping rather than a single clade.
facts.quote: Most phylogenetic analyses do not support the idea that all species of Asiatosuchus belong to their own clade
